div.head: TWO PILGRIMS ;
div.p: THE TWO PILGRIMS ;
LOVE AND GOOD DEEDS.
BY Corsr TOLATOI.
Two old men resolved to worship Unit in ancient Jerusalem. One was a rich mushlk his name was Yefim Taraimiteh Shevelef the other was not a rich man Yeli,t;i Bodrof.

letim was a sedate murbik ; did not drink vodka. nor smoke tobacco, nor take snuff. All his life long Ito hail never used a bad word, and he was a strict and upright man. Two terms Volta had served as etirosta. and had come out without a deficit. . .

family was large,---two sons and a married grandson, - -and all lived together. As for himself. he was hale, long-bearded, erect, and, though he was in his seventh decade, his beard war only be- ginning to grow gray. Yellsét was a little old man, neither rich nor poor in former times he had gone about doing jobs in carpentry; hot now, as he grew old, he began to stay at home, and took to raising bees. One of his sons had gone away to work, the other was at home. • Yelisei was a good-natured and jolly man. lie ' need to drink valise, and take snuff, and ho liked to sing conga; hut he was a peaceable man, and lived , amicably with his family and his neighbours. As to his person, Yelisib war a short, darkish lime ' milahik, with a curly beard and like his name- saint, Elirlia the prophet, he was entirely bald. The old men had long ago promised and agreed to ,go together, hut Tarisuitch had never found the leisure his engagements had never come to an end. As sOCPTI as one was through with, another began: first the grandson got married then they expected , the younger son f am the army; and then, again, . he planned to build a new One festival slay the old men met, and were sitting 1 in the sun.
: Well," says Yelit.tri, "when shall we set out to Jerusaltm,and fulfil our promise?' Yefitn knit his brow.... .. .

~....—.... ..... "We must wait a while." says he. "This year it'll come hard for me. I am engaged in building thi? isba. I counted on spending about a hundred rubles; but I'm already on the third, and it lent finished yet. You see. t barn take till summer. THE REV. 0, S. HEANEY ON MUSIC HALLS. The Rev. G. S. /Gamey, formerly minister of Wycliffe Congregational Church, Warrington, has, along with other ministers in Manchester, taken part in the agitation against the establishment of the proposed Manchester Palace of Varieties. Speaking at a meeting convened at the instance of the Paean ive Committee of the Manchester Branch of the Church of England Temperance Society, the rev, gentleman said that during his six years' resi- , dense in the East End of London he made it his business to go to every theatre and every sort of plate of entertainment he could find out, and it was quite impossible for him in the presence of ladies and, indeed, he might Nod it impossible in the pre- sence of men—to mention all that came to his knowledge with regard to music halls. Ito would not say the Palace of Varieties was intended to be such a place as he had seen in the East End, or a worse pines than those in the West End. but the tendency of all those places, as had been pointed out, was to drop down.— (Hear, hear.) People talked about religious cant, but there was a cant whieh was work than religions cant, and that was secular cant. People tallsol about theannisement of the working•mon, and said inn phanv AM. way," I have been to music halls and got no harm." Hut pMple were not always conseions of the hann they got in those places. Ile es-mid not say in any words lie muld find what he felt about musk halls. He would say nothing against theatres, and he was told that the Manchester theatms sea whole were well conducted, and that they had great talent upon the stage; bat there WVIT worse places in Nlanchttster than those could prve sibly be The matter of drink they regarded as the worst feature of musk halls. In the annt place, it formed the margin of profit for the proprietors. If it were not for the drink a great deal of the evils that I existed at the music hall would he very much mitigated. It gave a stimulus to debasing passion. He should like some of the gentlemen present I. go into Regent-street and the Villitechapel-road. London, when the musimitall doors let out their thouvmds. He had witnessed scenes I in Regent-st., at 12 o'clock at night,which had merle hire minder whether there was any Hovent in the land at all. lie could only liken it to a kind of immoral shamblm. No slave inarket in Egypt, no slave market that was ever depicted by paint, presented anything like the scene that wa.s b. bt, witnessed in Itegentsst. every ' night; and on Sunday nights that broad and grand boulevard id our great city was a perfect torrent of vice. And now Manchester was to have nne of thou, snusic- ' halls planted in her midst. If Lancashire men present had any grit in them, if Lancashire women had any womanhood, they would fiOtt this thing. Oh, David was a famous king, An' maister man o' singers His fiddle was a witching thing When touched by David's fingers But David never stirred a string To melody as fine, oh, And David's fiddle couldn't sing Like this owd hrid o' mine, oh ! My bonny little angel-neest, So tender, sweet, an funny. I wouldn't swap nr, music-kist, To own a mint o' money. I sometimes think it's gradely wick— There's a singin' brids inside on's. Oct one o=l.loo the late Dr. Barclay happened to dine in a large party, which was composed chiefly of medical men. As the wine-cup circulated, the conversation accidentally took a professional turn, and from the excitation of the moment, or some other cause, two of the youngest individuals pre- sent were the most forward in delivering their Opillioll9. Sir James Macintosh once told a poli - tical opponent, that so far from following his ex- ample of using hard words and soft arguments, he would pass, if possible, into the opposite extreme, mid use soft words and hard arguments. But our unfledged M.D.'s disregarded the above salutary maxim, and made up in loudness what they wanted in learning At length, one of them said : something so emphatic--we mean as to manner— that a pointer dog started from his lair beneath the table and bow- toove-uhrmed so fiercely that he fairly took the lead in the ditieustdoo. Dr. Barclay eyed : the hairy dialectician, and thinking it high time to close the debate, gave the animal a hearty push with his foot, and exclaimed, in good broad Scotch, w Lie still, ye brute; for I am sore ye ken lust as little about it as any o' them." We need hardly add, that this sally was followed by a hearty buret of laughter, in which even the disputants good- _turedly island. -

BEFRINN9ING THE 11011 ELEM.

A singular case of overcrowding was investigated at the Warrington Police Court, on Monday morn- ing, when a man named Richard Newton, who liven at 10, William-st, off School-brow, wan summoned for keeping lodgers without having a license entitl- ing him to do so. The wife of the defendant answered the Nummons, and pleaded guilty. Inspector Spinke spoke to visiting the houer of the defendant at three o'clock on the morning of Sunday, the Ifith inst., in company with Sergeant Cheney and Constable Caldwell, On approaching: the hmse, they saw a light in a pigeon cote belong- mg to the defendant, a small wooden erection about seven feet by live fcet. When tbeygot tothe house, the light in the cote went out, and they could hear that there was someone inside. Knowing that the cote belonged to the defendant, they knocked at tie door of his house, and Newton put his head out of the bedroom window. The officers were then admitted into the house. In the front room they found two beds, the first containing the defendant and his wife, and an infant eight months old. In the second bed were a youth, 16 years of age, and three girls, aged eight, six, and four years respec- tively. In the back room was one bed, in which ! was a young woman IS years of age. Downstairs, !in the front room, where there was no bedding • excepts mattraas and some old rags, the officers found ore man, one woman, two boys nine and five years respectively, and'four girls aged respectively 16, 13,1.1, and 11l years. This made a total of eight person, in that room-, all lying together the same as the lower animals." In the pigeon cote, in the yard, nine persons were sleeping. The place was in an extremely filthy state. Altogether, the officers found 2.5 persons-1f in the houst and nine in the pigeon cote. To use a common term—they were lying heads and taiis." - " ' ' '

1' to. Newton told the Bench the they had taken the children in for t.,e sake of eherity, as they were ming near the window. Twenty persons living in the &one yard were turned 041 t of their houses for owing back rent. End they bed nowhere to go. 'noir beds and mattrasses hadbeen put in the yard, ii Closets, and anywhere the people could put them. ; The Mayor: Was not there a Workhouse for them Ito go to.-- Mrs. Newton Some of them did go; four lof them went into the Union Alderman Davies: IHow long have these people been sleeping at your house Mrs. Newton: They only slept there that night.—lnspeeter Spinks said that th i e nformation ' of the police was to the effect that a great number of people had been sleeping in the house for several nights. That was why the visit was made._

'Aanitary-Inspector-'Norman said-tlZ'-the house was adapted for six persons. The women in the yard had told him that the agent for the property had gone there with a bailiff and turned them out of their houses. Ile saw the children there, and the furniture. Ile had seen furniture in the yard for four or five days, but altogether it was not worth half-a-soverign.Alderman Davies: We want to see how far the spirit of the law has been broken. Are thccre grounds in this case for her saying that it was to give these people shelter.—lnspector Nor- man said that he believed the statement of the woman was correct—Alderman Davies: It is not a lodging-house in the ordinary sense? --Inspector Norman: No. sir., -Alderman Harrison: It was not . for the purpdse of gain? Inspector Norman: I don't, think it was.- Mrs. Newton said that she only took them in for charity's sake, because the little chil- dren wore crying. She took them in about ten minutes to twelve on Saturday night, and the officers came at three o'clock in the morning. Alderman Davies said that the case was one of emergency, and the Bench considered that the defendatt should not have a penalty inflicted upon him. Mrs. Newton seemed to have acted under a kindly feeling. There was no doubt that the law had been broken, but under the circumstances the case would be dismissed, as the magistrates were satisfied that there had keen no intention of break- ing the spirit of the law. Inspector Spinks had done his duty in reporting the matter.--Mrs. New- ton It shall never occur again, sir.- Aldermen Davies: .1 think that, under the circumstances, the Sanitary Committee will be quite satisfied with our decision.

FIVE KILLED AND TEN INJURED.

NEW YORE, WEDNESDAY:A smiatts accident, due, , there is reason to believe, to gross negligence, occurred ! last everting. in the suburbs of Chicago, A well filled passenger train was running over the Rock Island line, when, onapproaching, it stowed down in response to signals Almost at the same moment a goods train be- longing to the Lake Shore line, overran the signals and dauhoef into the rear of the passenger train with great force. The last passenger ear was smashed to pieces, and of these inside five were killed outright and ten :seriously injured. Six men on the night shift at the Pendleton collieries of Mesn.s Andrew Knowles and Sins, Limited, were seriously injured on Tuesday night by the upsetting of a number of waggons in which they wore going down the engine brow on their way to the workings. Five of the men vote taken to the Salford Hospital for treatment. • One than succumbed to his injuries on IVednesday morning. The Salford District Coroner held an ineioest,on Thorn- day, upon the body of Jonathan Hall. Several of the men were injured, the deceased no seriously, that he died the some night at the Salford Royal Hospital. A verdict of "Accidental death " was returned.

div.head: QUEBEC CATASTROPHE.
div.p: THE QUEBEC CATASTROPHE.

The work of chairing the wreckage from the scene of tho great disaster at Quebec is now going on more rapidly, but the recovery of bodies is slow. The corpse of It. woman having been discovered under a vast Inasa of stone and rafters, efforts were at once made to extrigate it. The workers, however, in removing some of the beams, accidentally dislodged a huge boulder, which fell upon the bead of the unfortunate victim, crushing it to a jelly. Tllis incident serves to illustrate the great difficulty under which the rescuers have to work. Two more bodies were recovered on Saturday. Twenty corpses are now awaiting burial, and to thery the honours of a public funeral were on Sunday accorded. The total cumber of bedios recovered from the debris of the landslip inflow thirty, while thirty-six persons aro stilt missing. Many children are among the dead. There are some eams of whole families having j/erished.

div.head: UNIONIST LECTURER'S DISAPPEARANCE. ELOPEMENT WITH A YOUNG LADY.
div.p: THE UNIONIST LECTURER'S DISAPPEARANCE. ELOPEMENT WITH A YOUNG LADY.

The fears entertained regarding the fate of the Rev. A F. Barfield, Unionist lecturer and Baptist minister, of Walsall, have now (says a Birmingham correspondent) bon proved to he groundless, information having been received by his friends that the rev, gentleman has arrived in America, in company with a pretty girl, with whom, under the cover of his lecturing engagements, he has been carrying on an unministenal intngoe. It is Inhaled that for a couple of years the minister has regu- larly visited a lodging-house in Clapham, under the name of Wilson, To the husband of a preposse.ing young lady named Maggie Bourne. When ou his lecturing tours, Maggie u.atly travelled with him, or stayed at an hotel in the vicinity. It seems that his disappearance had long been prearranged, as in May last he wrote to the young lady at Clapham, telling her that he had had serious business losses, and wasgoing to America shortly and Maggie had hem preparing forthe voyage, whilst lie was:supposed to be resseiving, threattEning letters from Irish Invincible's, which now turnout to be self-eoneocted As Mr. and Mrs. Wilton, they took a passage by the steamship Ludgate Hill, and afterwards transferred their pa.ssage to the Allan line steamer Sardinian, which Sailed for Quebec on the 29th ult. Maggie, who is a girl of good education, is said to be of a bright, lively dis- position, and to e.ing anel play admirably. It is stated that among other artful schemes of the minister, he went in for Spiritualism, with Maggie as a medium. She was well-known in Walsall, where her father was for many years proprietor of some dining-rooms in High-st., where the rev, gentleman frequently went. A Walsall correspondent states that there is great unwillingness on the partof the friends of the Rev. A. F. Barfield to believe the story of his flight with a young, wonon, but she is known to have been a frequent corn- panion of his visits to various places in Staffordshire, and the companionship had caused surprioe and disparaging conments. Some months ago she spread a report that she was about to be married situ French nobleman of almost fabuloun wealth, and within the last few weeks letters have been received stating that the marriage had taken place, and that she and her husband were about to travel for five years. The " Birmingham Gazette "says :—There can be, no longer, any reasonable doubt that the di.ppearanee ii the Rev. A. F. Barfield, took the Penn of an elopement with Miss Maggie Bourne, under the circumstances already narrated. A member of our London staff callol, sn Wednesday, on Mrs. Gunn, of 72, Stanley-st., Clap- ham, with whom "Mrs. Wilson " lodged for some eighteen months or two years, having " Mr. Wilson" as I an occasional visitor. He took with him a cabinet photograph of Miss Maggie Bourne, late of Walsall, and the portrait was at once Identified n,o that of the lady who bade her an affectionate adieu immediately before starting for America on August 29. A portrait of Mr. Barfield had also been shown to her, and that in turn corresponded with the features of the "Birmingham electrician," in embarrassed circumstances, who had played the part of the lady's husband. Our representa- tive says i." The lady is described in almost affectionate terms by other residents in the house as to her manners and disposition, and there was nothing in the conduct of Mr. and Mrs. Wilson to distinguish them from an ordinary lawfully attached couple." One more, and 'almost superfluous, link in the chain of evidence against the absoinding pair is furnished in a telegram which was received from the Marquis of Ripon on Vi'ednesday. It will be remembered that it was a part of Miss Maggie Bourne's story to her friends that she had become acquainted with a French nobleman at Sutton Coldfield, that she met him on another occasion at Ripon (where the has a sister living), the" Cuunt " having been then on a visit to Lord Ripon at Studley Baal, and that she was married to this remarkable French aristocrat in July last, proceeding from London to Paris This tender fragment in the great romance was cruelly shattered by a, curt message, receivenl in reply to inquiries, fawn the Marquis of Ripon stating that, so far as he knew, there was no truth in the story.

div.head: LATEST WHITECHAPEL MURDER.
div.p: THE LATEST WHITECHAPEL MURDER.

On Tuesday, Mr. Wynne Baxter resumed the inquest at the Vestry Hall, Cable-street, Whitechapel, London, concerning the death of a woman unknown, whose trunk was discovered on the 10th inst. under the railway arch in Pinchin.st., Whiteehapel. John Clark, assistant to Dr. Phillips, divisional police surgeon, was the first witness called. and he described the position in which the body was lying when he first saw it, a few minutes after its discovery by the police. There were no signs of a struhgle lear the spot, and only a little blood which had oozed from the cut at the neck.. The garment which partly enveloped the trunk was of common make; it had been torn down the front, and had been cut out under the armholes,apparently with a knife. There were blood stain all over it, probably from being wrapped over the cut in the neck. Witness could find no distinguishing marks on the garment. Dm ecoposition of the body was just commencing. On examinins the body at the mortuary, witness concluded the deceased wcarian must have been between thirty and forty years of age, dark complexion. She had been dead about twenty-four hours. Besides the wound on the neck there was a cut about fifteen inches long through the external coats of the abdomen. On the back were four bruises, caused before death, one such as would result from a blow or kick. On the right arm were eight dis. tine. brain',, and ax yen on the left, all caused before death and of recent date. On the outer side of the left- arm was a out two inches long, and another lower down. The bruises on the arms might have been Wearfdorbz,trltuntltieliZetarwLere Tll.errl'erne'd were ! discoloured. Throughout the body there was an absence of blood, the heart being empty i and fatty. The stomach contained only a small quantity of fruit, and the liver was diseased. div.head: EIGHT HOURS MOVEMENT.
div.p: THE EIGHT HOURS MOVEMENT.

At Birmingham, on Monday, the Corporation Gas Committee had under consideration a report from the sub-committee mcommending the adoption of the eight hours system amongst the workmen at the gasworks, a system lately adopted by several of the London gas companies. The sub-committee were entirely in favour of the concession, and they recommended the adoption of eight hour: shifts, without any reduction of wages and with an equitable reduction of work. This recom- mendation the commitree have unanimously adopted. The decision will affect more than a thousand men employed as curb mixers, and will be an extra charge upon the Birmingham gus department of several thou- sand pounds a year.

div.head: MURDER AND SUICIDE AT GREENOCK.
div.p: MURDER AND SUICIDE AT GREENOCK.

A dreadful tragedy wa.s discovered at Greenock, early on Saturday morning. The dead lady of a young man and also that of a young woman were found in a garden, at Caddie-hill, both having evidently been killed with a revolver. The body of the young woman was covered with flowers, and Che body of the man was near by, M a kneeling position. A sm-chambered revolver was by his side, two of the chambers being empty. It appeared as though the man first shot the woman and then committed suicide. The polMe were at once in- formed of the discovery, and the bodies were soon identified as those of Andrew S. Walker, and his sweet- heart, a young woman named Holmes, daughter of a Greenock carpenter. They had been keeping, company for several years. The pair had a quarrel some time since, hut made it up recently. Walker was 23 and Miss Holmes 20.

FIGHT WITH CHINESE PIRATES. Letters front China give particulars of the dislodge- ment at Haipong of a strong hand of pirates who for five years past have occupied an island in the river from which they sallied forth on passing junks, and also levied blackmail on the neighbouring villages. In the dislodgement by the French forces thirty of the pirates were killed and some taken prisoners. The remainder succeeded in escaping to another island, where they are said to be still five hundred strong. Two Europeans were with them, one of whom at least was a Frenchman. The latter dropped his fan in Ins flight, and on it was the name Henri De Clausade, and above a coat of arms, and a count's coronet. De Clatmtde had deserted the French army, and had been acting as armourer to the pirates, preparing the weapons for the slaughter of his countrymen. The pirates left behind them a large quan- tity of arms and ammunition, including many Win- , chmter and Grass rifles. It is also said that an English- ; man is one of the gang.

div.head: DEATH OF MR. -WILKIE COLLINS.
div.p: DEATH OF MR. -WILKIE COLLINS.

The death is announced of Mr. Wilkie Collins. the novelist, which occurred at his London residence on Sunday night, at the age of sixty-five. Mr. William Wilkie Collins was the eldest son of the late Wm. Collins. RA., the well-known painter of rustic scenes. He was born in London, in January, 1824. His mother was a sister of Mrs. Carpenter, one of the best female portrait painters of the thee. After being educated at a placate school and spending two years with his parents in Italy, Mr. Wilkie Collins was articled for four years to a firm in the tea-trade. Exchanging commerce for law, he was a student of Linroln's Inn at the time of his father's death, and his earliest literary performance was an ad- minable biography of his father, with selections from his journals and correspondence, published in two volumes, 1848. Front this time Mr. Collins devoted himself en. tirely to literature. Mr. Collins' principal works have passed through several editions, both M this country and the United States, and iIa.VP been translated into French, Italian, German, Hutch, Danish, and Russian.

div.head: WOMAN'S SUICIDE AT NIAGARA.
div.p: A WOMAN'S SUICIDE AT NIAGARA.

A despatch from Niagara Falls, dated sth inst., re- ports that an unknown woman jumped into the river and paned over the Falls shortly before noon ontlnt day. The woman, who was dressed in dark clothes, was of light complexion, with auburn hair, and about twenty- five years of age, was seen walking carelessly towards the Niagara River, a short distance above Prospect Point. Soon after reaching the river she was observed to toss her hat and parasol into the water, and a moment later she glanced Iturrinlly arnund and deliber- ately leaped Into the Niagara Rapids. The mighty water caught her up liken straw and bore her rapidly towards the Atnerican Falls, fund first, her arms swing- ing in the air as she approached the brink of the Falls. Her face turned for a moment towards Prospect Point, not 20ft, away, hire was evidently up to this in full ! possession of her mind and uninjured. Just as she was ' passing over the Falls one erns was raised apparently to make a motion—eyes wide open. Otte moment of awful suspense, and the body was borne from view by I the rushing water. The captain of the Mail of the Mist shortly afterwards saw the body floating err the still water between American Fall and Canada Vreepark, hut before the boat could reach it the body had die- I appears,' fronts sight.

The definitive results of the elections for Paris are as follows :--Con.servatives, none ilooted ; Republicans, I ; Boulangist, 4 ; and second ballots, 37. div.head: Till,: EXAMINER. SATURDAY. SEPTEMBER 28. 1889.
div.p: Till,: EXAMINER. SATURDAY. SEPTEMBER 28. 1889.

Labour WE referred lost week to one or and two of the lessons of the Great Wealth. Strike, and urged the importance, in the interest of the poorest of the poor, of demands being made for the better remuneration A' the worst paid labour. It is gratifying to observe that no less an authority than Mr. GLAIWTONE has been impressed with the importance of the strike as a swial factor, and that he rejoices in its success sa tending to a fairer principle of division of the fruits of industry." Speaking at Hawanlen, on Monday, he said : I think that, looking at the condition of the labouring man, an enlightened and impartial observer, without reference to the rural districts, manufacturing districts, trade district, or any dis- trict in part icular,but casting hiseye over the whole field, will be disposed to think that, in the common interest of humanity, this remarkable strike, and the results of this strike, which have tendril to somewhat strengthen the position of labour in the face of capital, is a fact which we ought to regard with satisfaction as a real socinl advance (cheers), that it tenths to the greater, more uniform, more firm establishment of just relation amongst us; that it tends to a fairer principle of division of the fruits of industry. (Cheers.) Depend upon it, if that is the case it is a result that in of the highest importance, and one we may well congratulate our- selves upon; one that will tend to the ultimate strengthening of the bonds which unite the various portions of society together, and to the increase of the happiness and power of our country. (Cheers.)

It will be said by those who hold by the hard and fast lines of dry-as-duet political economy that sympathy of this kind is very cheap, and very mischievous, since it raises hopes which cannot be realised : that any idea of carrying the strike through by carrying it downward to those who allow themselves to be "sweated " almost out of existence most be given up as a fanciful dream. You cannot, the Political Economist will say, get more out of the Wages Fund than is to be found in the Wages Fund, and that fund is maintained not by strikes, but by the undisturbed operation of the law of supply and demand. But what if we grant this proposition, and say, . some of the East-end workers might say Very well ; we . have been working at the rate of a penny an hour ; but life is not worth having upon such starving ' terms. We' demandS that the payment shall be at least doubled ; and wo refuse to ' supply ' any more labour until our demand is conceded." Our own opinion is that, if those who are " sweated " so unmercifully could take op this position and stand together as the dockers stood, they would, before many weeks were over, win a victory all , along the line. The chief question is—can they; etrike, and strike effectively? The objector, how- ever, will say that that is not the chief question ; that the chief question really is whether the Wages Fund would permit of such a drain upon it. This is a plain, broad issue, and we propose to meet it. But first of all—What is the Wages Fund ? RICCARDO defines what he calls the "natural rate of wages," as "that which will maintain the labourer." Referring to this, Rum!. says "Maintain him! Yes; but how F—the question was instantly thus asked id me by a working girl to to whom I read the passage." How? After the fashion of swine—families herding in one room; . births and deaths taking place, and all the offices of life being performed,under the eyes of the young of both sexes? If the Wages Fund can afford nothing better than that, outraged humanity may be tempted, as Job was of old, to "curse God and die." Again we ask—What is the Wages Fund ? Is it the smallest possible sum for which the . Capitalist can get the Labourer to bend his back ? Or is it not rather a fair share of the fruits of industry—fair to the Capitalist as well as to the ! Labourer? We take it that not even the cast- iron Political Economist will hesitate to accept the latter statement. Let us see, then, whether the worst paid workers are getting their fair share —whether the Wages Fund is what it should he. A good deal has been said about the improved condition of the working and other classes during the past 50 years, and we are not going to deny that there has been improvement. Our contention is that the lot of the labourer pure and simple, and of those who may be called the "sweated "classes, has not improved proportionately, if it has improved at all ; and, what is immediately to the point,that this lack of improvement is not because there has been any lack of cash for the Wages Fund, in other words, the unskilled worker has been exploiteel he has been defrauded of his fair share of the fruits of his industry. During the past 50 years, there has been an increase in popu- lation in the United Kingdom from 26 millions to 37 millions. That is an increase of 42 per cent., and it is a iflatter of course to say that it has had its effect in adding to the pressure of competition. But when we turn to the increase of the nation's wealth during the name period, what do we find? Why, that the increase has been 124 percent., "or three times meter than that of the population ! " We gather from WWI, a recognised au- thority in nat. 1 statistics, that the aver- age rteennuilati"n of wealth was 73 millions per year before IMO: that it was 131 millions after that year; and that at the present time it may be safely reckoned at 150 millions. It is scarcely possible to realise what is meant by the country being richer every year by 150 millions of money; but this can be realised—that the labour- ing clawses are not getting their due share of it, and that, if "sweaters" are shockingly paid, it is not because the Wages Fund is in a low condition. Let us suppose that there are Five Millions of under-paid workers,to whom an advance in wages id 25. per week would be a Giabsentl. TWO shillings per week is, roundly speaking, £5 per year; and if the advance were given to Five Million workers it would mean just 25 millions sterling --25 mil- lions (ally out of the animal accumulation of 150 millions. It is no use suggesting, in view of such startling figures, that there is any great difficulty alma raising the wages of the lowest except that id the greed of gain. The money is made year by year: and the Wages Fund ,

SHOCKING TRAGEDY AT GLASGOW. WIFE MURDER AND ArrENVDED NUCIDE.

..... ....—......... .„. ..... . A terrible tragedy occurred at eight o'clock, on Thorn- ! day looming, m Maryhill, a suburb of Glasgow. An upholsterer named Murphy, suddenly cut his wife's throat, and afterwards performst a dike operation on himself. The woman is dead, ' and he was not expected to recover. NO reason is assigned. Murphy in quiet and imassioning. Ile in sober in habits. but has been out of employment. The people in the neighbourhood are quite surprised at what has happened. Murphy is severely cut aboutthe throat, butts thought at the hospital, to where be was taken, that he would recover. There in only one child a boy of seven. A later telegram says :—John Murphy, aged 28, labourer, employed at liearsden, !Hasgow, went home on Wednesday complaining of plins in his stomach. Nothing more was AIIM ,f him by the neighbours until this morn- ing, when he and his wife, of the same age, wen. found in bed with their throats cut and lockisl in each other's arms. The woman was dead, and Murphy was removed to. hospital inn speechless conditim.

Wsnter has set in early in Perthshire. On Wednesday morning the Grampians were covered with snow arid the weather was bitterly cold. Showers of hßil and sleet have Peen falling in the low-lying parts of the country for several days past.

Just before the close of the Session, cnb.,Lll'",r,. the Ins' h Secretary made some refer- .. .

ence to a measure which the Government proposed to bring in for improving rho higher education of the Roman Catholics of Ireland. It was understood that this meant the endowment of a Roman Catholic University. On all sides it was accepted that this waa the object of the Govermnent ; and it was thought by short- sighted people that it was a master-stroke of policy, in that it would have the effect of divid- ing the Irish Nationalists and the English Radicals. But it was now seen that the sword was a two-edged one, and that it was beginning to cut the Irish Secretary himself. Protestants were alarmed, and Orangemen indignant ; letters and resolutions have poured in upon Mr. BALFOUR, and in view of impending bye-elections Mr. BALFOUR bas had to climb down. He has this week written a letter to the Secretary of the Scottish Protestant Alliance in which he states that the foundation and endowment of a Roman Catholic University has never, no far as he is concerned, been in contemplation, and is not in his opinion, necessary. But as Mr. GLADATONR points out, it may be that the proposal is to endow a college; and if the college be large enough, it comes to pretty much the same thing. It is noteworthy, too, that Mr. BALFOUR says that he personally has not had a University in niind; for Mr. T. M. HEALY speaking on Tuesday, at the fortnightly meeting of the Irish National League, said :—" It wan well known to everyone who was in any way behind the scenes in politi., that at the time Sir M. Hicks-Beech left the Castle there was in the !pigeon-holes of his office a complete wham for a : Catholic University. It could not be denied that this was part of the programme that led to the Persico mission. It was a portion of the payment which was to be given to Rome for muszling Irish Catholic ecclesiastim." Mr. BALFOUR still sticks to it that he desires to "take steps to promote the higher University education of the Roman Catholic population ;" but we are inclined to think, after what has taken place, it will be fouhd to be one thing to desire and another to do. Roman Catholics cannot, at any rate, have any great faith in him, if they are not utterly blind; for whilst he shakes hands with them, se to speak, in one letter, gives them, in another, a slap in the face. Writing to Mr. Frani, he says:—

Let me call your attention to the fact that if the principles of the Separatist party were adopted, and the Irish were given full control over what are described as their own affairs, the Roman Catholic majority might employ the national funds obtained by the taxation of the Protestants as well no Catholics not only for promoting higher Roman Catholic education, but for the purpose of deliber- ately propagating Roman Catholic opinion amongst those who 110 not belong to that communion." And this is the man who desires to promote the I higher university education of the Irish people! Its would employ national funds, so he would have us believe, for such a purpose; but if a Home Rule Parliament were to act in this way it would be something abominable. Mr. BALTOrit is too clever by half ; he wants to run with the hare and hunt with the hounds. He is a JEMMY DIDDLBR, on this Catholic question, and is not to be trusted.
The French THE results of the Elections in Elections. France—so Inc as they have been

ascertained—are another illustra- tion of the famous saying of M. THEIRS that Republicanism least divides the French nation. General &MANGER had great hopes of securing a majority in his favour—hopes that might be re- garded as fairly well founded when he was returned at the head of the poll for a Paris constituency. But since then a good many things have happened, and amongst them fresh light has been thrown on the character of BOULANGER and Boulangisrn. The General has been tried and condemned by a public court ; and his policy, subjected to searching criticism, has been discovered to be one of "sound- ing brass and tinkling cymbals." For a poor man, he has had too much money at his disposal; for an honest Republican, he has had too many enemies of the Republic at his back. He Ina been found out in time, and France may therefore breathe freely in the assurance that General BOULANGER will not be Dictator just yet. The election returns are, it is true,. incomplete; there are many second ballots which will not take place until the 6th of October; but, mistiming that the Republicans will Ina as success- ful in the second ballots as they have been in the first—and there is no reason to think other- wise--it is certain that there will be a majority of undoubted Republicans so large as to over- power the combined forces of the Boulangists, the Monarchists, and the Bonapartista. The Genera himself has been returned; nut he will not be allowed to take his seat, as there is a heavy sentence hanging over him. and, apart from that, hohas been deprived of civil rights. His fortunesare therefore at a low ehb ; and nobody can be sorry that this is so who has at heart the prosperity of France. General BOULANGER has been a tool in the hands of those who are daily and nightly conspiring to over- throw the Republic; and it in satisfactory to per- ceive that he is a tool that has broken in their hands. The French have unhappily shown them- selves unable to rally to any one Premier for any length of time; and frequent change of Govern- ment has not unnaturally been taken as an indica- tion of the instability which is generally regarded as characteristic of our lively neighbours. But we must do them this justice, that, in the various crises they have passed through, they have at least shown themselves loyal to the Republic. They threw over MACMAHON when they found that they could not wholly trust him; and they have declined to be humbugged by BOULANGER. , Republican in the mass, they may quarrel amongst themselves, but they ore right in uniting to put down the enemies ofthe Republic.

The new act for the protection of children is , being put to good use. On Tuesday, at Halifax, a drunken mother was sent to prison for three months for wilfully neglect:ng her child. In threw months, the woman will have sobered down, and the child will probably have begun to look as a child should—plump and healthy.

A straw can show !how the wind blows; a trifling act may give the key to a policy. A Macelcrefield publican has been fined 5.:5 and , costs, and his license endorsed, for premitting Sunday " Nap." It is necessary in these eases to strike and strike hard, for, after a small fine, the I offenders cot and come :igen]. There are "Nappers" nearer home, but, although they have not yet I been caught, it is not to be supposed that this is because the police ever indulge in "nap."

It seems that some passengers who were waiting for a train at Broyhill, were ordered into a waiting room, and there locked in until the Queen's train went by. It would bewell if the passengers would test the legality of this proceeding by bringing an action for improper detention Breehin is not in Ireland; and, if people are to be locked up without rhyme or reason, it is well that they should know whether it is according to law.

This week, acting on the suggestion of a cones- ' pondent, we commence a story by Count Tolstoi, entitled The Two Pilgrims, or Love and Good Deeds." We commend it to the attention of our readers, as it is a good specimen of the great . Russian author's style, and of the doctrines he teaches. We take the tale, by permission from "Ivan Ilyitch and other stories" published by Mr. Walter Scott, Warwick-lone, London.

Sheffield butchers are agitating and protesting because the carcases of animals affected with ' tuberculosis have been declared unfit for human food. It is hard on them that they should now , and again be put to serious loss ; but it is harder on the public to have to eat deseased meat. The remedy of the butchers is to let each case be decided by a butchers jury ; but this would never do. Why not let a jury of milkmen decide as to adulteration in milk e

Typhoid fever still clings to St. Helens; and it has carried off several persons in the Runcorn ITnion. The latest victim at St. Helens is Mr. Henry Hudley, a cashier, 35 years of ago. The disease will spread if proper precautions are not taken; and honsehouldors will do well to see that their drains are clean, and in good working con- dition; that the milk they use is shove ampicion; and that their drinking water is pure.

There has been a contest at Kirkoswald, Ayr- shire, for the election of a clergyman. At one meeting there was a wrangle for over two hours. It is stated that "the proceedings exceeded in licence anything that has ever been witnessed at a Parliamentary election in the district, swearing and obscene language being freely indulged in. How delightful all this must have been to the candidatee and other godly people! Well, well, Scotland is not alone; there are numbers of people on this side the border who, though they do not go to Church, are ready to " swear " by it.

Mr. Chaplin, although a member of the Cabinet, either can't Or won't any anything about the pro- posal to endow a Roman Catholic University or College. He explained, at a meeting on Tuesday night,thatthe first authoritative statement he had seen was contained in Mr. Balfour's letters; that there had not been a meeting of the Cabinet sillce he became a member of the charmed circle and that he had only seen one Cabinet Ministry. Happy, innocent Chaplin! How glad he must be that in this matter he can profess to be as green as gram!

So it is not true that the Irish invincible, have "done away with' the Rev. A. F. Barfield, Union- ist lecturer. He has, to be sure, disappeared ; but he has turned up again in America. It is a ease,not of an Invincible, but of " Maggie by my side." He has run away with a pretty girl called Maggie Bourne ; but as Maggie has crossed the herring pond only, it cannot be said that she has gone to that "country from whose • bourn' no traveller returns." It seems that Maggie need to attend the reverend gentleman on his lecturing tours. He was evidently too much of a Unionist. " Sep- , aration " would have been hotter for both. A London beggar, named John White, under- stands his business. He has opened a banking account, and wee found the other day with a book in his pocket showing a balance to his credit in the Post Office Savings Bank of 1:27 lie. Ihl. He has gone to gaol for three months het what of that? The Government will take care of his money in the meantime. We may now uld to the ancient rhyme OF all the trade,. in England, the beggar's is the best, For when a matt is tired, he can sit him down and rest There is always something to he got, though lie. against the law ; And, with money in the Savings Rink, he doetint care a

straw. Unionists please note :--'4 Every train arrivin4 at Dolyhead and all the passenger steamer. to Dublin, are crowded with harvestmen going home. The railway and steamboat companies have made arrangements to newsy some thousands ef these passengers during the next few days." Shall we he tidies heretofore that Irishmen are idle sad improvident ? Or will the landlords of Ireland seise on thew hard-earned gains and say nothing?

The evidence showed that the deceased left liome on Monday morning with his horse and cart, and went to Itainhill for a load of coal. On his return journey he called about one o'clock in the afternoon at the Black Horse public-house in Famworth, and remained there until about thnv tieback. lie awn in !drink when he left, and shortly afterhe was found in the condition demribed on the road about half a mile from the inn hy Constable Burkin.—Mm. Ann Houghton stated that she lived in Cronton. On Monday afternoon, about ' three o'clock, shc was looking through her kitchen window on to the road, and she saw the deceased going ' along the road riding on the shaft of his cart. The ; owner of the clothes Patrick Davies, hail come to Warrington by train, and left his bundles in the waiting room while lie went to the Patten Arms to get a drink. WEAK RUE AT WALTON. On Tuesday, at the Daresbury Petty Sessions, Fanny Maddocks, of the Stag Inn, %3alton, was summoned for selling a pint of rum winch was adul- terated with :id per cent. of water. P.C. Crowder said be paid a shilling for the ruin, which he gave to Superintendent large, who forwarded it to Dr. Bell, county analyst, for analysis. Superintendent large: There was 3-1 per cent. of water ---or 9 per cent, more than allowed by the Act; 23 per cent. Is the standard allowed. -Defendant mid the did not mix the rum. Her servant, who was in charge • of the house during her absence, did so. She asked the officer to taken sample of everything else in the house, but be would not do m.- - The Chairman said the Bench were inclined to mks a lenient view et the case, after the explanation which Mrs.3laddocks had given, hut the offence must not be repeated. , Sire would be tined Is. and costs. ALLEGED Tunrr MOM A HUSBAND. On Thursday, at the Warrington Pollee Court, a woman named Elisabeth Ellimn. was charged with being drunk in Cockliedge-lane, and also with stealing from Samuel Ellison, her husband. two boys suits of clothes. his property. Mr. J. L. Whittle appeared to prosecute. Ile said the prosecutor was a very respectable man. and had been for about nine years a servant of the Corporation. Ile bad been married to the defendant about eleven years, but recently she had lived away from her husband and was in the habit of taking things from Inc house, On Monday she went to the house,broke AOMD of the windows and pictures on the walls, and took the two suits away. She afterwards pawned the clothes for 10s. Itsl., but at the same time redeemed some others, winch, she statml, were for one of the child- ren. The Clerk said he thought there was no inten- tion to steal, it was more a legal point as to whom the clothes belonged. The Bench inflicted a tine of 50. and ccste for being drunk, and bound defendant over to keep the putc, for six months.

It was alleged that prosecutor. who works at Bewsev forge, sem taking the beer home for slipper when prig- oners, who also work at the forge, came be- hind him, struck him on the face, knocked him down, and then took his hat and the bottle of beer. They were subsequently appre- Lended. The Bench said that the prisoners might Dave committed the offence more forth.' purpose of practical joking than anything else, but such con- duct could not he allowed. For the OSsatlit they would each he fined 40s. and costs, or a month's imprisonment with hard labour in default of pay- ment, and a conviction would be recorded against them with regard to the charge of felony.

It was also alleged that Michael Jeffries took part in the assault, hut POMP ot the witnesses said that they did not see him do to. It was stated that Michael used to be rather frequent in his appearances at the court as a defendant, but that he had for some time been teetotal. lie wan now, his wile told the magistrates, a credit to Warrington, as, indeed, were all the members of the family with the exception of John. After hearing the evidence, the magistrates dismissed the parents, and ordered the son to Mid a surety in 25, for his good behaviour, and to pay the costs. The head of the family. Michael, declined to make himself responsible for the conduct of his son. ALLEGED TRESPASS Is SEARCH OF GAME.

A LANCER ChARGED Willi CRUELTY. A SINGULAR CASE DISMISARG. tieorge Hearne, a private in the 9th Lancers, appeared at Daresbury Sessions, on Tuesday, to answers summons charging him with cruelty to a horse by working it whilst in an unfit state at Daresbury, on the 27th August. Inspector Nicholls, af the R.S.P.C. A., stated that at 11.45 on the morn- ing of the 27th ult., he was standing in the road outside that Court-room, when a troop of the fith Lancers, on their return from Wrexham to Man- chester, came up. The defendant was driving a squadron cart to which two horses were attached. Tbe animal on the off side was bleeding very much at the mouth. Its mouth and nostrils were covered with blood and the animal was evidently in much pain. Witness examined the horse and found that it was bleeding from two wounds. The off side of the bit wan pressing on what was really an abscess, which was broken open in two places. Mr. Robin- son, veterinary. surgeon. Warrington, said the wound was several days old. -Captain Charles Bishop, of the I, troop of the 9th Lancers, said that on the day in question he was in command of the troop, which had been to Wrexham, where it had formed an escort to her Majesty. Ito examined the horse, and found that it was suffering from what was called an ulcer. In was a port of gumboil which had broken. and he considered it was not an act of cruelty to work the horse, which had a very thick neck and was difficult to hold in. It was always bleeding at the month, because it" pulled 60 con- tinually, The defendant had no responsibility himself shout the condition of the animal, and was hound by witness's orders. Veterinary Surgeon Day. of the 9th Lancers, said he had examined the horse, and did not consider it necessary to stop it from working.- The farrier of the regiment was also called, and said be dirl not consider it cruel to work the horse. The Chairman said the magistrates thought the case a very trivial one, and it would be dismissed. Captain Bishop applied for the costs of himself, the defendant. and the witnesses. The Gov- Prnment allowed t hem no costs and witness bail Ind to come all the way from tlie North of Scat-, and to lie present that day. Ile apprehended there was no necessity for him to say more than that. In strictness that ought to be the whole of his application, becittme in every case 'of renewal now-a-days, a person, who was already the bolder of a licenne, could only be derived of it upon proper objection being sewed upon him seven days before the commtinceinent of the annual licensing meet- ing, or by as equally good objection being made specifi- cally to him in open court. In this case no notice of the objection had been given to 3ltillins at any tune, either seven days, or any other number of days, before the annual licensing meeting. No ohjection had ever been made in open court, and his client was, at the present 'leonine, quite ignorant of what the objec- tion was against the renewal of his license. The Bench had no power whatever to entertain any objection unless it had been sprcitically made in one 'of the two ways he had pointed out, and the applicant had had full opportunity of preparing his answer, and coining to meet the objeinion. There had been plenty of opportunity to make the objection, but it was now too late. Sir,—With the approaehof the winter eveCngs, the Sunday mustier in Sankey-st. is making its app.vance In full force. Tire crowds of young boys and girls who throng On- tine aiglifare, often behaving in a disorderly manlier, make it a matter of no little difficulty for qinetly dispowd people to lass along it anywhere between the bouts of eight and ten o'clock. The police do their duty as far as .• moving on" is concerned, butt an afraid they cannot do much good until a few of the delinquents age sunimorted before the magistrates. Of course, thia can only be done where there is behaviour of an unquestionably disorderly character. I don't want to new hard on the young people, and perhaps the authorities feel tne same way, but some deterrent in the way of making an example" is almost a necessity.-- Yours etc., Warrington, Sept. 25th, 1889.

Sir,—l have read with interest the correspondence which appeared in your ant week's hour, and I am please to SIT that Mr. tiandy's letter has bPell so ably supported by "Cymro" and Mr. Roberta. From what little I have been able to see of Tolatoi's writing:, they well merit the complimant which Mr. Gandy has paid them. Novelists are plentiful now-a-days, and the literary market is more or less glutted with their several productions—good. bad and indifferent. But whilst the majority of these may, perhaps, lay claim to be enter- taining, and amusing, how few of their works instruct the mind, or rather, I would my, breathe forth any pod purpose. If I am to understand that a "religious fanatic" is one who desires to see Christianity made more practical, and its maxims carried more fully out insole dealings with our fellow men, and not merely a thing to be shut up within the walls of a church or chapel, or a topic for devines to cavil over, then I say the more we have of them the better it will be both for the progress of Christianity itself—and for the moral and social advancement of the world at large. For in my opinion much of the crime of to-day is the direct out- come of our social wrongs. am, yours, she., Frodsharn, Sept, 24th,
-"'EXNIO."

Sir,—Seeing there are to many opponents in the field against Mr. Peers, and taking a deep interest in the subject matter of Mr. F. R. Roberts' letter, I should like, by your permivsion, to reply to it. My motive in doing so is not no much to aitiist Mr. Peers in an attack upon Christianity in its purest form, but rather to enforce a widely spreading conviction that, if the teachings of Christ are to take their proper place in the religion of the future, they must be stripped at all that is mysterious and irrational.

The Brotherhood of the Living Christ may be accepts able to reason, but the Godhead of the Crucified 1. 1,. total conflict ; Unitarianism has been teaching this for many years, and it is undoubtedly making great progress, for we have it on the high authority; of Mr. Spurgeon, " That the Churches of to-day are shot through and through with Unitarianism." . . _ . . . .

Now for the argument ; in the first place, Mr. Roberts wishes to imply that between the old and new versions of the parable there is an important difference. Now, this is not so, for both versions run exactly in the same words with the exception of the substitution of' Had." and ° anguish" for Heil " and " torment. ; "it may ken distinction, but it is without a difference. 'use rich num is still sent to a Hell of dame and torments, for the plainly. ntated reason that he had received a sufficiency of good thing i this life, %lint right ha. the Church, with its inferences an, enneccelonei to come between me and Christ ? Are not His words !mffielent ? There is not one word about the man's morality, good or had. and we conclude that the sum total of his offence was, that he lacked the poverty which Lanarus possessed. Tas ; Christ meant what He said, and therein lien a lair ; to my acceptance of His divinity. Utifortunatelv for Mr. Roberts, this is not the only instance of Christ's teaching that the possession of riches is fatal to a man's salvation ; " Ye cannot serve God and Mammon." " Lay not up for yourselves treasures on earth." These are plain enough, but the plainest of all is Christ's advice to the rich young man, the moral man, the man who had listened to Moses and the Prophets, and had kept their commandments and the law One thing thou lackent •, go and sell all thou bast, distribute to the poor ; then shall thou have treasure in Heaven." lam aware that orthodoxy puts a different interpretation to these passages than is war. ranted by the facts ; it draws upon the imagination in order to harmonine with the church's ideal of Christ. Whoever refuses to be drawn becomes, like Mr. Gandy, unsound in his orthodoxy. , • •• • ' • •

Bt the most rt of M. Roberta's letter lies in his admission that .• a millionaire has no place in Christian society ; neither has a beggar." This latter portion is evidently, slip of the pen, for it surely is too uncharitable to be Christian. ...to the first, tie Christ's teaching over again, for it follows if a rich man is not fit for Christian societ), he is not fit for heaven.

In conclusion, allow me to say that an honest, straight- forward opinion on any subject, sacred or secular, is far better than that miserable reseryation,which is a bane to our social and religious life, but which. I ant sorry to see, Mr. Roberts deems so advisable. —I remain, yours respectfully, Latchford. Sept. 24th, 1889.
DONOVAN.

MORE ABOUT THEOSOPHY. Sir,—Mr. W. H. Butler contributes a letter to your imue of 21st inst., headed Theasophie Dogmas," and I would like to comment upon this letter as briefly as possible. Mr. Butler does not wish to go into the alleged I exposure of Madame Blavatsky. Why then does he refer I to it at all, seeing that I made no mention whatever of this lady, ready as I am at all times to undertake her defence as I would my own ? His intention is doubtless to make the innuendo without formulating the charge. Madame Blavatsky is well accustomed to this sort of attack from Christian " champions.

I repeat that Theomphy attaches no efficacy to any creed whatever, but this a not saving that Tkeosophists believe nothing, nor is it saying that conduct may not be influen.A for good by 111P0II$ of creed. The meaning my words obviously bear in that the simple po.easion of any creed cannot have any saving power, and Mr. Sutler must know that what I said had special reference to the doctrine of substitution.

Mr. Butler enumerates a number of ...tides- which he extracts from my "creed," and be wishes to examine my proofs. Of course, he knows very well that it is int- possibleto advance proofsin metaphysical matters. What he wishes to know is, I presume, upon what grounds I and others have arrived at certain conclusion. I will try to give him a rough outline of these grounds. Medical science has shown conclusively that in certain conditions of bodily prostration perceptions may be received other than aensuou.ly. A ifs of absolute- altruism is followed by the same result, bat to an infinitely higher and purer degree. Every bodily desire being subdued, the higher prmciples can act far beyond the narrow limits set by the senses. We believe that there are men who, by purity of life and rigid/discipline. have reached an elevation at which absolute knowledge takes the place of theenV. Anyone who is familiar with the phenomena of clairvoy- ance, and the astounding powers which may sometimes be met with even in the West, will readily be able to conceive of a vast extension of this power of perception. Sages who liner attained to this stage of open-perception to a greater or a lesser extent may be found in well-nigh every religion, Christianity by no means excepted. Let it not be imagined, however, that Theosophy om- elets in open-mouthed na:eption of statements on author- ity. Although certain conclusions have been accepted by the majority of Theosophists, the published objects of the Society are sufficiently wide to refute any attempt to saddle a creed upon as. Mr. Butler asks--" hoes Theosophy offer anything lIPW p" I reply emphatically " No." What it offers for consideration is the united testimony of sages and mystics of every rareand of every religion, and it confidently amens that this testimony will be found well-nigh unanimous on the main points. If Mr. Butler wants a convenient guide to Thcseaphr, he will find it in his New Testament, and especially in the "Sermon on the Mount '' If he wants mysticism, let him turn to the writings of Paul, and ask himself why Christians no longer live the life which Paul recom- mended. Does Mr. Butler suppose that Theosophy I. in opposition to Christianity? I will answer hit, that it ii Christianity, and yet is far,l A' older than tbe religion

now linown by that name. St. Augustine says, what Snow called the Christian religion has mist,sl among the enemas, and was not absent from the beginning of the human race unit Christ came in the flmh ; "and this n•ligivn we wish to revive, which in the living hear; of every modern faith. - -

Theosophy does not requireany creed from its unalibers, Wave does urge them and all men to lead the life where- by the truth -shall become manifest to then,. It urges them to subdue the lower nature, to heoune unselfish, to love their 'fellows, and it promises them that. if they will du these things, they shall reach au elevation and a knowledge of which they have not dreamed. We wish to win no man from his religion, but we wish him to search out the heart of that religion, and obey its teach- ings. We otter no hashed up Buddhism as a remedy for materialism, but the knowledge that comes from altruism. A belief in Re-iticunation,or in anything else, does not make a inan a TheowThist. hell-denial and , self-purification alone can do that. Does Mr. Butler wish ' fur evidence or any particular theory which I, or other heosoplkista, have advanced? lieu I shall be glad, with Iyour permission, to do my best in that direction. It is obvious, however, that space will not permit MP to deal with so vast a subject in any exhaustive manner.— Yuan truly,

Sir,—When a man thrusts Ids fingers into my disk uninvited he cannot complain if he gets his knuckles rapped. Now, then, one at a time. lamat a loss to know what Vindex "teak up his pen to vindicate, unless it was the utter want of compre- hension he has shown. There are people who require an intellectual abacus "to enable them to grasp idean readily assimilated by ordinary minds. I thought that even the "meanest capacity" would have seen, from the context and the association of the name of Malthus, that the.. orer-production " was the overlrodnetion of children, which I think even " %Index" most see would tend to lower wages. On a subject like this I was averse : to going into details in a public print. Surely, when II said that the sins of the fathers were visited upon the ! children, I had at least indicated what was meant. Mad Cyinro," as well as" Vindex," the least literary insight, they would not have perpetrated a blunder sogross, open, and palpable.

Ant.," Cyinro," I rather admire that sweet little touch as to Voltaire and Ingersoll llst Cyniro "is much behind the times. The "odium theologicum " which I these names might once have called forth is now dead I and buried, or is found to exist only in the ignorant or vulgar. I should have had more respect for' Cymru's" ' judgment had he stuck more closely to the text of my letter. and not drawn so very freely upon a wild and I untrained imagination. Where, for instance, does lie find use advocating" restrictions upon marriage, and a forcible seizure of the income of the married ?" Surely he must have been reading between the lines ; a practise I in which he appears to be an adept, apparently oblivious of the psychological fact that in so doing we are almost eertainte see therein our own words and ideas rather than the author's. But this is not the only wild idea for which Cymni is responsible. It appears that he would be a divider and diatributer—of other men's yawls. He says, a sma II portion of(" Dives! ") wealth would have made i Laaarua comparatively comfortable." Very true, and the place of Lazarus at Dives' table would be tilled by ' lanother beggar who in turn must be bought off? And so to s finish ! What a grand scheme for rendering thriftlessness perennial, and placing a premium upon shiftlesileAs ! Can "Cymro "be the joiner I ham heard of who, when plaining a board, fell to complaining about this same unequal distribution of the world's ' goods? "fiat." said he, "if I was a law maker I'd divide the money of the rich amongst as poor folk." I When asked what he would do when his sham of the spoil was spent—"Oh, then we'd divide again" he replied ! Was it not Artemus Ward who was no augiousto Shed every drop of blood—of all his unites and aunts— in defence of his country? ••Cymride," mode of reliev- ing the poor might be. to him, a very cheap and ea.sy one, but would not have the merit of permanency or general acceptability. As to Mr. F. It. Roberts,of whom I have no personal knnwledge. I take him to be the leading light in noise Sunday School. If not he has missed his vocation. His inaccuracies, and freedom of interpretation, might pass current then; unchallenged. but look rather shaky When published to the world. I need only notice one para. graph. It is a gem, with or without "nesting." He says, it If Mr. Peers will consult the Revised Version he will find there is no such contrast in the destinat ion of the two as is implied in his bahl statement, bald, and untrue as well, inasmuch as it conjures up before the minds of your readers the aensuous scenes of a popular, but unacriptural heaven, and the horrors of a rpular, but equally unseriptinal, hell." The rest of this precious paragraph will be dealt with in my reply to Mr. Gandy. Well, I have consulted the Revised Vareion, and can find no essential difference between them. In both, Lazarus, from no cause assigned, except that he MIA poor, was—to put it scripturally—. carried by ange/s into Abraham's Wisorn." whilst Dives, equally from no muse assigned, except that he was rich and enjoyed his riches, WM consigned to. place where —seriptinally—he was' in torment in this flame," or, in the language of the Revision," in anguish in this flame." Now, where is the difference between the sensuous, the popular and the scriptural account ad this place of torment 1 Has Mr. P. R. Roberts been reading between the lines? Pedlars he will give us the result of his reading, and show where in any essential point the two differ. This gentleman is one of a ela.ss who— finding how very absurd a literal interpretation of many i passages of acripture. appear when viewed by modern eyes, have raised the parrot cry of their being unscrip- total ! In this way any passage may be regarded as I unricriptural—if you read het wren the lines and hlink the lines themselves. In this connection, will Mr. F. R. Roberts say, when next he favours us with hises-,sithedcu utterances, whether he can constientiouslv avow entire belief in the creation, temptation, and fiat of man as detailed in I. Genesis, and this without interlinear read- ings adapted and modified no beautifully to suit the idiosoicraciea of the reader? But let it be taken as Matthew Arnold's plain man "would understand it. My friend Mr. Gandy confesses himself surprised, and I think might have asidecl,ennfnsefl. He has not given himself time for reflection. In his haste to pose as a Christian apologist, he indulges in vague generalities, and when he condescends to particularise he becomes I inarcurate, lists the Dives-Laranis episode, he says "that Jesus never intended to convey any such impreis Ann. Such an idea, I feel sure, would not occur to one , person in a thousand. It certainly never occurred to , me, and, before reading Mr. Peers's letter, I never heard of anyone drawing such an inference from the story." I Sin, reading the above. I have taken the trouble to look un the comments on this parable in Dr. Adam Clarkids Bible. The whole of the noes on this passage would be too long to quote, but the IP, sums up thus—. An Christ has described this man. does he appear culpable? What I are his crimes? Why, I.—Fle was rick. was .nely clothed. And lII—He feasted well. No other evil ; is spoken of him. In comparison with thousands he was I not only blameless, but he was a virtuous man "—stove are the Dr.', words and his italics. . . .

Hut I will waive my privilege of criticising my friend's other diacrepancies. and come at once to the main point at issue ,yiz . —ls Tolstoi a reliable guide to foinw in dea - inc with this vast question of Poverty and Riches? His method is, I premium from kin works, based upon Christianity. Let on see what kind of Christianity it is : he builds upon! Like Mr. Handy, Tolgtoi ia not ortho- dox. He, TolMoi, not Mr. Handy. will have nothing to do with the dogmas of the Pall, of original sin, and of • eternal punishment." That is, he cannot accept as an article of belief the account of the fall of znan from a state of innocenreasnarrated in Genesis. In common with mnst reading people who are acquainted with the more than doubtful source of these puerile traditions, b • rejects them as unworthy of belief. The earliest known records of them early attempts at guessing the origin of life and of evil is found in the clay tablets .if the Shumio-Arcadians—a nation that stool to the Chat. dons very much as the ancient Britons stand to us. And these wedge-shaped characters, impressed upon thetie once mft pieces of clay, are now the oldest known literature of the world. Front this early literature, I " " '

.... think there can he no reasonable —doubt. the no-ca 11..-1 Mosaic arc:omit of creation and the Fall of Man was I copied almost literally. So Tolstoi rejeetn the Biblical account of the Fall an an idle fable. Yet upon this unntable ground 'elan the Christianity as taught in the churches to-day. There we are taught that Christ died to redeem mankind from the consequences of that Fall. Now, it is obvious at a glance, that if the Fall had no existence an • fact, any affnmption or inference based upon it an a fact, must lose credit equally with the fable upon which it was founded. Now. I think none will dispute that the we is of Christ indicated a belief in the reality of the Fall as an historical fact—indeed, the purpose to which he devoted his whole life nhowed his entire acceptance of that amount. Logically, if the Fall. be a foundationless fic- tion, the Crucifixion was a purposeless waste of suffer- ing, and any hopes and belief founded upon it an baff- leo, as the fleeting fancies of a dream. And here the inquirer han to chose one of the two alternation. The hintnrie person we know as Chrint accept.' and believed this (abut.. Fall to have been an actual occur- fence—or—but the other alternative it sueh a very unpleasant one that I forbear to state it. Now. not even Tolffoi hitnself would maintain that the onto begotten Son of Infinite Windom could be miffaken or tinder an illusion in • matter no important ! So the logical conclusion Is that the historic personage I we know an Christ wan mistaken in proclaiming himself I the Son of God; the rejection of the dogma of the Fall is , the premise to thin ennelusion. Thin, oat natural con- NNUMICP, brings this historic person into the ranks of moral philonophers. Teachers. and Social Reformers, a titan whew origin wan as that of other men, the non of Mary, the wife of Joseph, the carpenter ; him to whom priests and dogmatistn f all Christian ages have as-

My contention with regard to Tolstoi is that in matters of practical moment, like this moote Poverty and Riches, a man who aecepts the premises—i.r.—denies the Fall— and still accepts the conclusion—i.e.—accepts Christ as s Divine teacher, cannot be considered a safe and satisfac- tory guide. BRE'NNER, M.P., AND HIS WORK-

_ MEN. On Saturday, Mr. Brunner, M.P., addressed the workmen of Messrs. Brunner, Mond, & Co., as they were leaving the works at Winnington. He said he . had heard that Mr. Champion, of the Labour Elec- tor," had decided to come amongst them in order to get up a strike, but they were all aware that he had broughtan action for libel against Mr. Champion for what he had said about him. He had said the work- men wens being downstrisiden.and bad been termed the "Whits slaves of Wilmington, but whet had angered him (Mr. Brunner) was the assertion then his late father had isuportnt wretched foreign paupers to work at starvation wages. and to live like pigs. Ile spoke in favour of trade unionist prine*l., and said that , nothing would please him better than that they ' should band themselves together for their own good. In concluding, Mr. Brunner said that I whether Mr. Champion came or not, he was glad to : have had the opportunsty of speaking to them ; and he I continued What is it that I lay before you ? Thnw I good ruln—straightforward, honest combination in the form eta Trades Union ; a determination never to deal with any question of trade except by open negotiation ; a determination that you will not, until all open and straightforward negotiation has been exhausted, resort to the last desperate remedy of a strike. Gentleinen, ask from you a definite declaration :—Are you in favour of the three principtes—combination, negotiation, and fairplay (Loud enes of " Y..") Will you give me a show of hands ? la, every man's hand held up, and I am thankful for it. I felt satisfied when I got up this morning that I could trust you, and I hope, gentlemen, that you now feel that you can trust me. (Loud al:I- I pLsuse.l

The advantage of collecting the Runcorn general district rate in two half-yearly instalments, instead of annually, was amply made manifest at a meeting of the Commissioners on Thursday. During the past six months there is a nett increase of .£702 4s. 24. in the assessment, and as the rate for the ensuing six months will be levied upon this additional sum, it is a clear gain to the town of about .r. 35. Mr. Imisoffs prediction, when advocating the scheme, is thus borne out tc the letter, and the appointment of Mr. J. I). Jones to the position of rate collector, about which some cf the ratepayers were inclined to cavil at the time, is fatly justified by the result. . . . . .

Oreat interest has been taken in the proposal to increase tbe salary of the Master of the Runcorn Alnion tip the cum of ne a year. Opinions were divided on the subject, and while guise argued that he was amply pa his services, others argued that he ought to b" better recompensed for his labours. There is as a fine muster of Guardians at the Workhouse on Tuesday, 29 out of the 42 members being present, whilst the usual attendance does not average more thins dozen. As Chairman of the Finance Com- mittee, Mr. Bmndreth championed the Master's cause, and showed conclusively that although be was managing the house efilcientlyand economically he received a much inferior salary to the late mas- ter. Vs farmers," as Mr. Whit/ow is so fond of remarking, had, however, come with minds made up against any advance, and the result was a defeat of the Finance Committee's recommendation by 14 votes to eleven.

—After this busbies, had been disposed of the I muter and the schoolmaster had a hot five minutes, but fortunately they were absent and their feelings were spared. These officers, it appears, have been unable to amicably fulfil their duties together. and the Guardians have had to deal with complaints emanating sometimes from one and sometimes from both, but always aimed at each other. The Board have at last decided to call on the aid of the Local Government Board to decide the disputes, and upon them will devolve the duty of saying which is the guilty one,or whether, in the words of Mr. Whitlow, "one is W. bad LP the other." Somebody is bound to suffer. There ion rumour afloat that an attempt will be made to effect 'compromise in the forthcoming elec. tion of members of Widnes:3o9°l Board. At present the Board consists of five Churchmen, live Cat holies, and one Nonconformist, and the basis of agreement mentioned is to constitute the Board of four Churchmen, four Catholics, and three Nonconform- ists. The difficulty of deciding who shall retire in favour of the two new members will probably offer an effective bar to any compromise ; and the chances are in favour of a contest. With a proper organisation there ix no reason why the Noncon- formists should not secure three representatives in a fair battle, but hitherto they have displayed a lamentable lack of cohesion, and have consequently all but gone to the wall on each occasion. They should take example by their friends the enemy.

div.head: PROI;OSED NIGHT. SCHOOL.
div.p: PROI;OSED NIGHT. SCHOOL.

Mr. Braid°, head master of the Ship Canal school at Thelwall, is about to open a night school for the benefit of the Ship Canal employes in that neighbourhood. Reading, writing, arithmetic, dmwing, and composition will be taught by an efficient staff ot teachers, and as the school fee will only be one penny per week, the facilities offered will, no doubt, he readily made use of, and the school well supported by the residents. ^'OE ASSESSMENT OF THE BRIM,— CANAL.

Scalars ACORN,. .—On Monday morning an nankin- nate occurrence happened to one if the joiners, named Joseph Gibbs, engaged with others In setting up the new machinery in the Frodsham Bridge Floor Mills. It seems that whilst removing a flour dressing machine with levers, it gave a sudden jerk, and crushed the man against the wall, with the result that Ike was rendered unconscious. It was found necessary to convey him to the Infirmary at Chwters PAROCHIAL Consorram.—At the monthly ifleeting of these C,nonmitteen, held m the Town Ran, Frodsham, last evening week, for. Robinson presiding in the alwence of the Chairman, the Clerk read a report and produced plan of sections of sewer at llooth-street. Frodsham, prepared by Mr. C. R. Linaker, surveyor, from which it a, peared that an additional length of sewer would be required to carry away from that street the sewage satisfactorily, when it was decided that a specification be prepared and estimates obtained as to the cost of the hkwer. A letter was also read from Mr. A. E. Pollard, asking the nom- mittee to extend the sewer in Smithy-lane a distance of about 80 yards, in order that he might connect the drains frOM certain biases which he intends to erect on land abutting on such lane. Collier, of Hobby, proposes to erect MI land near to the Methodist Free Church. It was resolved that the plan submitted he approved. The Inspector of Nuisances reported several eases of over- crowding in the district, and stated that he had served the requisite notices for their abatement.
